--- title: "Hypothesis Testing" format: revealjs: logo: /images/lmjl.jpg footer: "Data Science with R · " include-in-header: - text: | - text: | width: 1280 height: 700 margin: 0.03 center: false auto-animate-duration: 0.9 slide-number: true number-sections: false code-overflow: wrap code-annotations: select chalkboard: true include-after-body: - ../../../resources/slidecrafting/spread-script.html - ../../../resources/slidecrafting/mono-whitespace.html - ../../../resources/slidecrafting/logo-link.html - ../../../resources/slidecrafting/paper-adv-popup.html theme: [default, ../../../resources/slidecrafting/styles_template.scss, ../../../theme/scss/ensai-theme.scss] revealjs-plugins: - codewindow - tabset filters: - arrows - roughnotation - zoom-vp - ../../../resources/slidecrafting/code-pop.lua knitr: opts_chunk: dev.args: { bg: "transparent" } lightbox: true --- # Statistical Framework ## The testing game **Goal.** Use a finite sample to confront a working assumption $H_0$ (*null hypothesis*) against a competing one $H_a$ (*alternative*), and decide which one the data support. **The engine.** A **test statistic** $T(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ that you can always compute, and whose distribution you (approximately) know **assuming $H_0$ is true**: the *null distribution*.
$\Longrightarrow$ Extreme values of $t_0$ under $H_0$ argue in favour of $H_a$.
## Asymmetry {.build} **Warning.** The game is **not symmetric** in the two hypotheses. > - The whole procedure rests on what happens **when $H_0$ is true** (we know the null distribution); > - It says nothing at all about $H_a$, which is left completely unspecified.
You only ever *calibrate* the test under $H_0$.
# Test Statistic ## What a statistic must do A good test statistic $T(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ should: - take **real values**, computable as soon as you observe the data; - be such that, **under $H_0$**, small values comfort $H_0$ while large values raise suspicion **in favour of $H_a$**.
*Optional but very useful:* an accessible (asymptotic) distribution under $H_0$ in *classical* assumptions, e.g. normality.
## Example: testing a mean {.build} **Model.** $X_1, \dots, X_n$ *i.i.d.* $\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, with $\sigma$ known. Test $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ vs $H_a: \mu \ne \mu_0$. **Test statistic.** $$ T(X_1, \dots, X_n) := \sqrt{n} \frac{\overline X - \mu_0}{\sigma}, \qquad \overline X := \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i . $$ **Why it works.** $\overline X$ is unbiased for $\mu$, so under $H_0$ it concentrates near $\mu_0$ and $\;T$ stays small; departures push $T$ to large *positive or negative* values. ## Where the null distribution comes from Four ways to learn the distribution of $T$ under $H_0$: - **Parametric.** A theoretical distribution, from distributional assumptions on the data. - **Asymptotic.** The theoretical distribution of $T$ as $n \to \infty$ (large sample). - **Bootstrap.** Approximate the distribution by resampling, in a large-sample regime. - **Permutation.** Approximate it by permuting labels, in a low-sample regime. ## One-sided vs two-sided {.build} **What raises suspicion.** Skewing what *large* means changes which tail(s) of the null distribution matter: - **one-sided:** only the right tail ($\mu > \mu_0$) or the left tail ($\mu < \mu_0$); - **two-sided:** both tails ($\mu \ne \mu_0$). We always reject $H_0$ only when $t_0$ lands in the **tail(s) that argue in favour of $H_a$**. ## Right tail: $H_a: \mu > \mu_0$ $$ T(X_1, \dots, X_n) := \sqrt{n} \frac{\overline X - \mu_0}{\sigma} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/right-tail-test.jpeg){fig-align='center' width=230} ::: ::: Large *positive* $T$ points to $\mu$ truly above $\mu_0$.
$\Longrightarrow$ Reject only in the **right** tail.
## Left tail: $H_a: \mu < \mu_0$ $$ T(X_1, \dots, X_n) := \sqrt{n} \frac{\overline X - \mu_0}{\sigma} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/left-tail-test.jpeg){fig-align='center' width=230} ::: ::: Large *negative* $T$ points to $\mu$ truly below $\mu_0$.
$\Longrightarrow$ Reject only in the **left** tail.
## Two tails: $H_a: \mu \ne \mu_0$ $$ T(X_1, \dots, X_n) := \sqrt{n} \frac{\overline X - \mu_0}{\sigma} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/two-tail-test.jpeg){fig-align='center' width=230} ::: ::: Extreme $T$ in *either* direction raises suspicion.
$\Longrightarrow$ Reject in **both** tails.
# Making a decision ## You can be wrong Every decision can miss, in two ways. - Rejecting $H_0$ wrongly: **Type I error**; - Failing to reject a false $H_0$: **Type II error**. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Decision \(H_0\) is true \(H_a\) is true
Do not reject \(H_0\) Well done Type II error
Reject \(H_0\) Type I error Well done
````` ::: ::: **Remember.** Only the **Type I** rate is controllable, because it is a probability computed *assuming $H_0$ is true*, the very frame we adopted. ## Significance level $\alpha$ **Control the Type I error.** Force $\mathbb{P}_{H_0}(\text{reject } H_0) \le \alpha$, where the bound $\alpha$ is the **significance level**. **For a right-tailed test**, "reject $H_0$" is the event $T > x$, so the rule becomes $$ \mathbb{P}_{H_0}(T > x) \le \alpha \iff F_T^{(H_0)}(x) \ge 1 - \alpha . $$
$\Longrightarrow$ Reject when $t_0 \ge q_{1-\alpha}$, the order $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of the null distribution.
## p-value **Definition.** The **p-value** is the probability, *assuming $H_0$ true*, of observing the data we got or data *even more in favour of $H_a$* (here with $t_0$ the observed statistic): $$ p = \begin{cases} \mathbb{P}_{H_0}(T > t_0) & \text{right-tailed} \\ \mathbb{P}_{H_0}(T < t_0) & \text{left-tailed} \\ 2\min\!\big(\mathbb{P}_{H_0}(T > t_0),\, \mathbb{P}_{H_0}(T < t_0)\big) & \text{two-tailed} \end{cases} $$ **Decision.**
$\Longrightarrow$ Reject $H_0$ when $p \le \alpha$.
## The decision at a glance ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/pvalue-alpha.png){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: Reject $H_0$ when $t_0$ is extreme enough that $p \le \alpha$. ## Statistical power **Definition.** The probability of *correctly* rejecting $H_0$, i.e. of rejecting when the alternative is right: $$ \gamma := \mathbb{P}_{H_a}(\text{Reject } H_0) = 1 - \beta . $$ **Why it matters.** - It compares competing testing procedures; - In trials (clinical, crash tests), it calibrates the **sample size** needed for a target power. **Caveat.** Computing $\gamma$ forces you to step *under $H_a$*, which is often only vaguely specified, so power studies explore how it behaves across plausible alternatives. # Compliance testing ## Testing the mean, $\sigma$ known **Model.** $X_1, \dots, X_n$ *i.i.d.* $\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$. **Test.** $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ vs $H_a: \mu \ne \mu_0$ (or $>$, or $<$). $$ Z_n = \sqrt{n} \frac{\overline X_n - \mu_0}{\sigma} \stackrel{H_0}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1) $$ **Check.** $\sigma$ must be known to compute $Z_n$; the generic R helper is [`t.test()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/t.test.html). ## Testing the mean, $\sigma$ unknown **Workaround.** Plug in the *empirical* standard deviation $S_{n-1}$ for $\sigma$. $$ T_n = \frac{\overline X_n - \mu_0}{\sqrt{S_{n-1}^2 / n}} \stackrel{H_0}{\sim} \mathcal{S}tudent(n-1), \qquad S_{n-1}^2 := \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \overline X)^2 $$ **R function.** [`t.test()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/t.test.html)
$\Longrightarrow$ Knowing $\mu$ *vs* $\sigma$ swaps a $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ for a Student law with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
## Testing the variance **Model.** $X_1, \dots, X_n$ *i.i.d.* $\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$. **Test.** $H_0: \sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2$ vs $H_a: \sigma^2 \ne \sigma_0^2$ (or $>$, or $<$). **Candidate statistic.** $$ U_n = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(X_i - \mu)^2}{\sigma_0^2} $$ **Hitch.** $\mu$ is unknown, so we cannot *compute* $U_n$ as written. ## Testing the variance, $\mu$ known **Workaround.** When $\mu$ is known, the statistic is computable and has a $\chi^2$ law: $$ U_n \stackrel{H_0}{\sim} \chi^2(n) $$ **R function.** none (built from scratch). ## Testing the variance, $\mu$ unknown **Workaround.** Plug in the empirical mean $\overline X_n$ for $\mu$. $$ U_{n-1} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(X_i - \overline X_n)^2}{\sigma_0^2} \stackrel{H_0}{\sim} \chi^2(n-1) $$ **R function.** none (built from scratch). ## Testing a proportion **Model.** $X_1, \dots, X_n$ *i.i.d.* $\sim \mathcal{B}e(p)$; $X_i$ records whether individual $i$ has the feature. **Test.** $H_0: p = p_0$ vs $H_a: p \ne p_0$ (or $>$, or $<$). $$ B_n = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \mathcal{B}inom(n, p_0) \quad \text{under } H_0 $$ **R function.** [`binom.test()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/binom.test.html) # Two-Sample Testing ## Framework Compare the distributions behind **two independent samples**: $$ X_1, \dots, X_{n_X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2), \qquad Y_1, \dots, Y_{n_Y} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y^2) $$ with the two samples statistically **independent**.
Two questions: equal variances? equal means?
## Testing variance equality **Test.** $H_0: \sigma_X^2 = \sigma_Y^2$ vs $H_a: \sigma_X^2 \ne \sigma_Y^2$ (or $>$, or $<$). $$ V_n = \frac{S_X^2}{S_Y^2} \stackrel{H_0}{\sim} \mathcal{F}isher(n_X - 1, \, n_Y - 1) $$ **R function.** [`var.test()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/var.test.html) **Validity.** relies on normality and independence within and between samples. ## Testing mean differences **Test.** $H_0: \mu_X = \mu_Y$ vs $H_a: \mu_X \ne \mu_Y$ (or $>$, or $<$), with $\delta := \mu_X - \mu_Y$ and $\delta_0$ the value under $H_0$. **R function.** [`t.test()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/t.test.html)
The form of the statistic depends on whether the variances are equal.
## Mean differences, equal variances With $\sigma_X^2 = \sigma_Y^2$, pool the two sample variances: $$ T_n = \frac{(\overline X_n - \overline Y_n) - \delta_0}{\sqrt{S_\mathrm{pooled}^2 \left(\tfrac{1}{n_X} + \tfrac{1}{n_Y}\right)}} \stackrel{H_0}{\sim} \mathcal{S}tudent(n_X + n_Y - 2), \qquad S_\mathrm{pooled}^2 := \frac{(n_X-1)S_X^2 + (n_Y-1)S_Y^2}{n_X + n_Y - 2} . $$ ## Mean differences, unequal variances (Welch) With $\sigma_X^2 \ne \sigma_Y^2$, keep the variances separate: $$ T_n = \frac{(\overline X_n - \overline Y_n) - \delta_0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{S_X^2}{n_X} + \dfrac{S_Y^2}{n_Y}}} $$ ## The Welch degrees of freedom The null distribution is a Student law with the **Welch degrees of freedom**: $$ T_n \stackrel{H_0}{\sim} \mathcal{S}tudent(m), \qquad m = \frac{\left( \dfrac{S_X^2}{n_X} + \dfrac{S_Y^2}{n_Y} \right)^2}{ \dfrac{(S_X^2 / n_X)^2}{n_X - 1} + \dfrac{(S_Y^2 / n_Y)^2}{n_Y - 1} } $$ # Adequacy testing ## Goal Adequacy tests check whether the observed data are **coherent with a given probability distribution** $F_0$. ## Shapiro-Wilk test **Test.** $H_0: (X_1, \dots, X_n) \stackrel{i.i.d.}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ vs $H_a:\ \text{not normal}$. $$ T_n = \frac{\left( \sum_i a_i X_{(i)} \right)^2}{\sum_i (X_i - \overline X_n)^2} \stackrel{H_0}{\sim} \mathcal{W}ilks(n) $$ **R function.** [`shapiro.test()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/shapiro.test.html) — needs $3 \le n \le 5000$. ## Kolmogorov-Smirnov test **Test.** $H_0: X \sim F_0$ vs $H_a:\ \text{not } F_0$. $$ T_n = \sup_{x \in \mathbb R} \left| F_n(x) - F(x) \right| $$ **Asymptotic null distribution.** $$ \sqrt{n}\, T_n \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}} \sup_{x \in \mathbb R} \left| B(F(x)) \right|, \qquad B\ \text{a Brownian bridge} $$ **R function.** [`ks.test()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/ks.test.html) — asymptotic. ## $\chi^2$ adequacy for one categorical variable **Idea.** Compare observed class frequencies with the theoretical ones under $F_0$ ($k$ classes, $f_i = n_i/n$). $$ U_n = n \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{(f_i - f_{0i})^2}{f_{0i}} \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}} \chi^2_{k-1-\ell} ,\qquad \ell = \#\text{parameters estimated for } F_0 $$ **R function.** [`chisq.test()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/chisq.test.html) — needs $n_i \ge 5$ typically. ## $\chi^2$ independence between two categorical variables **Test.** $H_0: \nu = \mu \otimes \lambda$ (independence) vs $H_a:\ \text{dependence}$, where $\nu$ is the joint law and $\mu, \lambda$ the marginals. **Statistic** (with $N_{\ell, \cdot}$, $N_{\cdot, h}$, $N_{\ell,h}$ the row/column/cell counts). $$ U_n = n \sum_{\ell=1}^s \sum_{h=1}^r \frac{\left( \frac{N_{\ell,h}}{n} - \frac{N_{\ell,\cdot}}{n}\frac{N_{\cdot,h}}{n} \right)^2}{\frac{N_{\ell,\cdot}}{n}\frac{N_{\cdot,h}}{n}} \xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}} \chi^2\big((s-1)(r-1)\big) $$ **R function.** [`chisq.test()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/chisq.test.html) — asymptotic; typically $n \gg 30$ and $N_{\ell,h} \gg 5$. ## Your turn - Download the lab `10-Hypothesis-Testing-Exercises.qmd` from the course website. - Run the proposed tests with R and interpret each p-value in one line.

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
